==Problem 21==
Charlotte the spider is walking along a web shaped like a <imath>5</imath>-pointed star, shown in the figure below. The web has <imath>5</imath> outer points and <imath>5</imath> inner points. Each time Charlotte reaches a point, she randomly chooses a neighboring point and moves to that point. Charlotte starts at one of the outer points and makes <imath>3</imath> moves (re-visiting points is allowed). What is the probability she is now at one of the outer points of the star?

[[File:2026 amc 8 q21.png | 450px]]

<imath>\textbf{(A) } \frac{1}{5}\qquad\textbf{(B) } \frac{1}{4}\qquad\textbf{(C) } \frac{2}{5}\qquad\textbf{(D) } \frac{1}{2}\qquad\textbf{(E) } \frac{3}{5}</imath>

==Solution 1==

The graph undergoes '''rotational symmetry''' meaning when scaled on a factor <imath>k</imath>, here <imath>k = 5</imath> of the points, it is the same as considering a fixed starting position of Charlotte. WLOG let this starting point be the topmost one. On the second turn, she cannot be on an outer point. Then she is forced to an inner point in a 1 chance. From any outer point, she must move to an outer point with a <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> chance. Finally, from that outer point, she must move to an inner point with <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> chance. Therefore, the probability is <imath>\boxed{\frac{1}{4}}</imath>.

In general, the probabilistic depends on if the pentagram is on some <imath>n</imath>th moveset. For instance, <imath>p_0 = 1</imath>, and all <imath>p_n = \frac{1}{2}(1-p_{n-1})</imath>. The term <imath>(1-p_{n-1})</imath> is of the point that to get to an outer point one must come from an inner point. 

~Pinotation

Note to SquishBJ from Pinotation: You are absolutely correct, thank you for taking the time to review my solution. Constructive counting is a swing and miss here due to the fact the question doesn't ask for strict tournaments rather cases based on dependency. Good catch :>

==Solution 2 ==
We begin by noticing that from an outer point, the next move must be to an inner point as both adjacent points are inner. Next, there are four adjacent points - two are inner, two are outer. Thus, there is a <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> probability for both. The final move depends on which type of point was the last one - if it was outer, the next one would have to be inner, so that gives us a probability of <imath>0</imath> for an outer point. However, if it was inner, there is, again, a <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> probability that the next one is outer. Therefore our final probability is <imath>1 \cdot (\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \boxed{\textbf{(B) } \frac{1}{4}}</imath>.

~OlympiadMaster

==Solution 3 (Markov Chains)==
Note that there are only two states due to five-fold symmetry. Hence, we can create a Markov Chain with two states: outer and inner points. Transitioning from an outer point to an inner point happens with probability <imath>1</imath>, and transitioning from an inner point to an outer point happens with probability <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>. The spider always changes from states, and it never stays on the same state in two consecutive moves. The spider starts on an outer point, so the probability at Move 0 for outer points is <imath>1</imath>.

Enumerating the values for 3 moves using our recursive rules above:

<cmath>\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
&&\\
\textbf{Move} & \textbf{Outer} & \textbf{Inner}\\
&&\\
\hline
&&\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
&&\\
\hline
&&\\
1 & 0 & 1\\
&&\\
\hline
&&\\
2 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2}\\
&&\\
\hline
&&\\
3 & \frac{1}{4} & \frac{3}{4}\\
&&\\
\hline
\end{array}</cmath>
We aim to find the probability of the spider being at an outer point on Move 3. Thus, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B)} \frac{1}{4}}</imath>.

~Reese's Pieces

==Solution 4 (Recursive)==
Let <imath>p_n</imath> be the probability that Charlotte is at an outer point after <imath>n</imath> moves.

From the symmetry of the star graph we derive that the probabilities are:

* Outer <imath>\to</imath> Inner with probability <imath>1</imath>
* Inner <imath>\to</imath> Outer with probability <imath>\frac12</imath>
* Inner <imath>\to</imath> Inner with probability <imath>\frac12</imath>

If Charlotte is at an outer point after <imath>n+1</imath> moves, she must have been at an inner point after <imath>n</imath> moves and then moved outward. Therefore
<cmath>
p_{n+1}=\frac12(1-p_n)
</cmath>

The initial condition is
<cmath>
p_0=1
</cmath>
since she starts at an outer point.

Rewrite the recurrence as
<cmath>
p_{n+1}=\frac12-\frac12 p_n.
</cmath>



First, we find the constant equilibrium solution <imath>c</imath>:
<cmath>
c=\frac12-\frac12 c
</cmath>
<cmath>
\frac32 c=\frac12
</cmath>
<cmath>
c=\frac13.
</cmath>


<cmath>
q_n=p_n-\frac13.
</cmath>

Substituting into the recurrence,
<cmath>
p_{n+1}=\frac12-\frac12\left(q_n+\frac13\right)
=\frac13-\frac12 q_n.
</cmath>

Thus
<cmath>
q_{n+1}=-\frac12 q_n.
</cmath>

We now have a clean equation.
<cmath>
q_n=q_0\left(-\frac12\right)^n.
</cmath>

Now we do some simple algebra.
<cmath>
q_0=p_0-\frac13=1-\frac13=\frac23,
</cmath>
<cmath>
q_n=\frac23\left(-\frac12\right)^n.
</cmath>
<cmath>
p_n=q_n+\frac13=\frac13+\frac23\left(-\frac12\right)^n.
</cmath>

Now we plug in <imath>n=3</imath>:
<cmath>
p_3=\frac13+\frac23\left(-\frac12\right)^3
=\frac13-\frac1{12}
=\frac14.
</cmath>

Thus the probability Charlotte is at an outer point after <imath>3</imath> moves is <imath>\boxed{\frac14}</imath>.

~JohnnyAppleseed

===Remark===
This solution turns a recursive sequence into a geometric sequence. It's overkill for this question, but it could be used if we are finding the probability after a large number of moves, e.g., 2026 moves.

~TheRealMee

==Solution 5 (Quick)==

Like solution 1 and 2 we know that we can choose one edge point to start on. From any edge point there are two possibilities to go to, we can just use one of these possibilities due to symmetry, making the problem easier to solve. Once we go to this point we can see that there is a <imath>\frac12</imath> probability that you go to an edge point and a <imath>\frac12</imath> probability that you stay in a center point. If you go to an edge point there is a 0 probability that you can end on an edge point. While if you stay in the middle, there is a <imath>\frac12</imath> probability that you go to an edge point on your 3rd move. We can calculate this using symmetry without loss of generality making this problem much easier to solve. Finally our answer is <imath>\frac12*\frac12=\frac14</imath> which is <imath>\boxed{B:\frac14}</imath>


(PS. Make sure to check whether you can use symmetry for a counting problem before you actually use it.)
~SShreyas
